title: Emotions as Products of Ideas
summary: Emotions as consequences of value-judgments, not as tools that discover facts.

lessons.title: Products of ideas
lessons.objective: See an emotion as a consequence of a value-judgment you already hold, not as a first fact about the world.

exercises.prompt: In this unit, an emotion is a product of what?

choices.text: Ideas you hold, in the form of a value-judgment
The facts themselves, with no judgment in between
A special sense that discovers what is
A vote of the people around you

feedback.note: An emotion follows from ideas: a value-judgment about something as for you or against you. It is not a raw piece of the world.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to the role this unit gives it.

pairs.right: A consequence that follows
An estimate of for or against
The premise the estimate rests on

feedback.note: Ideas support a value-judgment. The emotion is what follows from that judgment. None of the three is a substitute for the facts.

exercises.prompt: Complete the unit's basic claim.

parts.text: An emotion is a consequence of a value-

feedback.note: The word to hold is judgment. The feeling is the consequence, not a sensation standing in for a conclusion, and not a group vote.

exercises.prompt: Build the claim in the order this unit teaches it.

feedback.note: Emotions follow value-judgments. They do not discover facts. Leave the distractors out.

exercises.prompt: What is a value-judgment, in this unit?

choices.text: Your estimate that something is for you or against you
The color of an object, with no evaluation
The date on which something happened
The mere fact that your heart is beating

feedback.note: A value-judgment evaluates: for or against, gain or threat, good or bad by the ideas you hold. A bare color, date, or pulse is not yet that estimate.

exercises.prompt: Match each feeling to the kind of value-judgment it follows.

pairs.right: Judgment that something is a gain
Judgment that something is a danger
Judgment that a gain is a loss

feedback.note: The same kind of event can be met with different feelings because the value-judgment differs. The feeling tracks the estimate, including a mistaken one.

exercises.prompt: What has to change if a mistaken emotion is to change?

parts.text: behind the judgment, and the emotion that follows can change.

feedback.note: Emotions are products of ideas. A new weather report, crowd, or calendar date does not rewrite the judgment. A revised idea can.

exercises.prompt: Say what an emotion is not.

feedback.note: The feeling is real as a feeling, but it is not a first fact about the world. It arrives after an estimate.

exercises.prompt: Two people feel differently about the same event. This unit locates the difference in what?

choices.text: Their value-judgments about the event
Two different events, despite the shared description
A difference in eyesight alone
The clock time of the event

feedback.note: One event can be judged as a gain by one person and as a threat by another. The emotions follow those judgments, not a second copy of the event.

lessons.title: An estimate, not the facts
lessons.objective: Distinguish what a feeling reports — your estimate of the facts — from what it does not report: the facts themselves.

exercises.prompt: What does a feeling tell you, on this unit's account?

choices.text: Something about your estimate of the facts
The facts, apart from any estimate
What other people are thinking
The future, as a finished record

feedback.quote: What you feel tells you nothing about the facts; it merely tells you something about your estimate of the facts.
feedback.note: The feeling is news about your estimate. It is not news about the facts.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, interview with Alvin Toffler, Playboy, March 1964

exercises.prompt: What does a feeling tell you nothing about?

choices.text: The facts
Your estimate of the facts
That you hold some evaluation
That you are feeling something now

feedback.quote: What you feel tells you nothing about the facts; it merely tells you something about your estimate of the facts.
feedback.note: You can know that you feel something, and still learn nothing about whether the estimate matches the facts.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, interview with Alvin Toffler, Playboy, March 1964

exercises.prompt: Match each term to what it reports.

pairs.right: Your estimate
What is, apart from that estimate
Whether the estimate holds

feedback.note: Keep the three jobs apart. The feeling delivers the estimate. The facts are what the estimate is about. Only a check can tell you whether they agree.

exercises.prompt: Finish the contrast.

parts.text: of the facts, not the facts.

feedback.note: Estimate is the right word. The feeling does not create the facts, deny them, or replace them.

exercises.prompt: Build the report a feeling actually gives.

feedback.note: Stop at estimate. Adding the facts would turn the feeling into a report it does not make.

exercises.prompt: You are furious because you think a friend lied. Then you learn they did not. What did the fury tell you?

choices.text: That you had judged the act as a betrayal
That the lie had happened
That anger is how lies are discovered
That the facts rearrange to match the fury

feedback.note: The fury reported the estimate: betrayal. When the facts differed, the feeling did not become evidence that the lie occurred.

exercises.prompt: Match each feeling to the estimate it reveals.

pairs.right: An estimate that missed the threat
An estimate that treated it as danger
An estimate that the gain is good

feedback.note: A feeling can fit the facts or miss them. In every case it still reports the estimate, not a separate look at the facts.

exercises.prompt: Intensity does not settle the question.

parts.text: The emotion can be intense and the

feedback.note: A louder feeling is a stronger report of the estimate. Volume, pulse, and weather do not turn that estimate into a fact.

exercises.prompt: State the limit on intensity.

feedback.note: How strong the feeling is does not measure how true the estimate is.

exercises.prompt: After a strong feeling, which question fits this unit?

choices.text: What estimate of the facts produced this?
Which fact did the feeling prove?
How do I vote the feeling into reality?
Which fact can I skip because I already feel sure?

feedback.note: The useful question asks for the estimate. The feeling did not prove a fact, enact one, or license you to skip one.

lessons.title: Not a tool that discovers facts
lessons.objective: Reject the claim that emotions are tools of cognition — means that discover facts.

exercises.prompt: Are emotions tools of cognition?

choices.text: No. They do not discover facts
Yes. A strong feeling is a way of knowing
Yes, whenever the feeling is sincere
Yes, but only about other people's ideas

feedback.quote: Emotions are not tools of cognition.
feedback.note: Sincerity and strength do not turn an emotion into a means of knowing facts.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, interview with Alvin Toffler, Playboy, March 1964

exercises.prompt: What would a tool of cognition do, in the contrast this unit draws?

choices.text: Discover or identify facts
Follow automatically from a value-judgment
Speed the heart for a moment
Name how you feel, and stop there

feedback.note: Cognition here means identifying facts. An emotion follows a judgment you already hold. That is a different job.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to its job in this unit.

pairs.right: Not a tool of cognition
What actually discovers facts
The estimate the emotion follows

feedback.note: Do not hand the emotion the job of identifying facts. That job belongs to a means of knowledge. The emotion registers an estimate already made.

exercises.prompt: Complete the rejection in the unit's own terms.

feedback.quote: Emotions are not tools of cognition.
feedback.note: The rejected role is cognition, not a bodily process like digestion or a change in the weather.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, interview with Alvin Toffler, Playboy, March 1964

exercises.prompt: State what emotions do not do.

feedback.note: The sentence to build is the ban: emotions do not discover facts. That they follow judgments is a different claim, saved for another line.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, I feel it, so it is true. What are they treating the emotion as?

choices.text: A tool of cognition
Only a consequence of a judgment
A hint to go check the judgment
A report with no evaluation in it

feedback.note: Using the feeling as proof treats it as a tool that discovers facts. This unit says it is not that tool.

exercises.prompt: Match each practice to what it does with an emotion.

pairs.left: I feel it, so it is true
pairs.right: Treats the emotion as cognition

pairs.left: I feel it, so I hold some judgment
pairs.right: Reads the estimate

pairs.left: I identify the facts, then judge
pairs.right: Does not use the emotion as the tool

feedback.note: Reading off your estimate is allowed. Treating the feeling as the discovery of the fact is the move this unit rejects.

exercises.prompt: Give the rule for proof.

feedback.note: A feeling is not proof. Proof has to identify the facts by a means that is not the emotion.

exercises.prompt: Which practice stays inside the unit?

choices.text: Identify the facts by some means other than the feeling, then look at the judgment the feeling reveals
Skip identifying the facts whenever the feeling is clear
Let the stronger feeling outvote the facts
Use the feeling to invent a fact that was not there

feedback.note: The feeling can show you an estimate you hold. It cannot take the place of identifying the facts.

lessons.title: The judgment comes first
lessons.objective: Trace the order: idea and value-judgment, then emotion. The feeling does not come first and then invent the judgment.

exercises.prompt: In the order this unit teaches, what comes before the emotion?

choices.text: A value-judgment based on an idea
The emotion, which then builds the judgment
A wish that the facts would change
Other people's feelings, averaged

feedback.note: Idea and value-judgment come first. The emotion is the consequence. It does not reach backward and invent the judgment.

exercises.prompt: Match each step to its place in the order.

pairs.right: The premise you hold
The estimate of for or against
The consequence that follows the estimate

feedback.note: Read the order downward: idea, then value-judgment, then emotion. Reversing it makes the feeling look like a discoverer.

exercises.prompt: Name what comes first.

feedback.note: Judgment first. Applause, weather, and echo are not steps in this order.

exercises.prompt: Build the order in one line.

feedback.note: Use the tokens that put judgment first. The extra copies would reverse the order.

exercises.prompt: Can you summon an emotion as a way of learning a new fact?

choices.text: No. It follows a judgment; it does not go out and discover
Yes. Decide to feel the answer, and the fact appears
Yes, if you feel it before you hold any idea
Yes, if enough people feel it with you

feedback.note: There is no emotion prior to the ideas it expresses. You cannot use a feeling as a scout that brings facts back.

exercises.prompt: Match each approach to the order it uses.

pairs.left: Wanting the offer to be fair before you look
pairs.right: Feeling standing in for inquiry

pairs.left: Looking first, then judging the offer
pairs.right: Facts, then judgment, then emotion
Treating the consequence as the inquiry

feedback.note: Looking first respects the order. Stopping at the feeling, or feeling the verdict before you look, puts the consequence in the place of inquiry.

exercises.prompt: The feeling does not lead the idea.

feedback.note: Precede is the error. The feeling also does not outvote, erase, or paint the idea. It comes after the idea's value-judgment.

exercises.prompt: Reject the reversed order.

feedback.note: The feeling does not come first. It does not invent the world either, but that is a further claim. This line is only about order.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, My anger proved he was wrong, before any look at the facts. What went wrong?

choices.text: The consequence was used as if it had discovered the fact
Anger is not a real emotion
Anger is always a correct value-judgment
A value-judgment is never allowed

feedback.note: Anger can be a real consequence of a judgment. The mistake is the order: treating that consequence as the discovery that he was wrong.

exercises.prompt: Which sequence matches the unit?

choices.text: Idea, value-judgment, emotion
Emotion, then the idea the emotion invents
Emotion, fact, and no judgment at all
Fact, emotion as the proof, judgment optional

feedback.note: Hold the sequence idea, value-judgment, emotion. The other lines let the feeling discover or replace the judgment.

lessons.title: When feeling and fact clash
lessons.objective: When a feeling and a fact conflict, re-check the value-judgment instead of treating the feeling as evidence.

exercises.prompt: A fact and a feeling conflict. What do you re-check first?

choices.text: The value-judgment that produced the feeling
The fact, until it matches the feeling
The emotion, used as a measuring instrument
Whether you are allowed to have a feeling at all

feedback.note: The feeling can be real and still rest on a bad estimate. Re-check the judgment. Do not edit the fact to suit the mood, and do not pretend feelings should not exist.

exercises.prompt: The feeling is vivid. Does that make it evidence of the conflicting fact?

choices.text: No. It is evidence of the estimate, not of the fact
Yes. Vividness is a kind of proof
Yes, if you would rather the fact were different
Yes, if someone else feels it too

feedback.note: Vividness shows the estimate is live. It does not show that the estimate matches the fact it clashes with.

exercises.prompt: Match each situation to the next step.

pairs.left: Feeling clashes with a checked fact
pairs.right: Re-check the value-judgment

pairs.left: Feeling fits a fact you have checked
pairs.right: The estimate may be right
The feeling is not a conclusion about the world

feedback.note: A fit does not make the emotion the tool that found the fact. A clash sends you back to the judgment. With no check, you only know the estimate.

exercises.prompt: What must you refuse to edit?

feedback.note: The facts stay as they are. The mood is what the judgment produced. Applause and the calendar are not the things under review.

exercises.prompt: Say what to re-check.

feedback.note: Re-check the judgment. Do not rewrite the world so the feeling can stay in charge.

exercises.prompt: A value-judgment about a real danger is correct, and you feel fear. What is that fear?

choices.text: A fitting consequence, still not the tool that discovered the danger
The tool that discovered the danger
Proof that every emotion is a mistake
Something you must shut off before you may act

feedback.note: A right estimate can have a fitting emotion. The emotion still did not do the discovering. The judgment did, after the facts were identified.

exercises.prompt: Match each case to the standing of the emotion.

pairs.right: The emotion can fit the facts
The emotion can be strong and still off
The emotion did not discover the fact

feedback.note: Fit and mismatch are both possible. Discovery is not. The emotion remains a consequence of the judgment.

exercises.prompt: How do you change a mistaken emotion, on this account?

feedback.note: A mistaken emotion yields when the value-judgment changes. Turning the volume down, waiting on the weather, or polling an audience does not revise the estimate.

exercises.prompt: Build the practical line.

feedback.note: Fix the estimate, and the feeling can follow. Ignoring the facts is the opposite move.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is this unit's summary?

choices.text: Emotions are consequences of value-judgments, not tools that discover facts
Emotions are tools that discover facts, and judgments come later
Emotions should be eliminated because they are never consequences
Emotions become facts when enough people share them

feedback.note: Hold the summary as one claim: consequences of value-judgments, not tools that discover facts. The feeling is not a mistake for existing, and a crowd does not convert it into a fact.

sources.quote: Emotions are not tools of cognition.
sources.citation: Ayn Rand, interview with Alvin Toffler, Playboy, March 1964

sources.quote: What you feel tells you nothing about the facts; it merely tells you something about your estimate of the facts.
sources.citation: Ayn Rand, interview with Alvin Toffler, Playboy, March 1964
